extraction_notes.note: Long case-by-case computations of ideal generators and projective-module bases in running text ("Explicit computation shows ...") were emitted as semi_formal claims that feed the following lemma's proof.
Subsections 5.1 and 5.2 ('Proof of Theorem P main (i)/(ii)') are section-filling proofs; each lemma+proof block is one setup step, and Theorem P main is split into part claims ClP for (i) and (ii).
Numbered 'Remark' that sketches the proof of the cited idempotent lemma; typed proof rather than remark.
Sentence both cites Skowronski Thm 3.8 and defines 'standard'; kept as an external theorem.

Section and theorem numbers are produced by \refstepcounter{thm} paragraphs, so many numbered paragraphs ('3.4.', 'Remark 4.9.') are prose; the label F BD sits on such a paragraph and resolves to a section, so its \ref edge was added by hand.

Setup sentences ('From now on, ... it suffices to check ...', 'We write Lambda'(T(l,m)) = KQ(l,m)/I and recall ...', the description of Q_T^(2)) and the table of algebras A_1...A_16 (kept only inside Theorem P theorem standard nondomestic) were not split into nodes.

nodes.name: Classification of self-injective cellular algebras of polynomial growth
nodes.section: Introduction
assumptions: $K$ be an algebraically closed field of odd characterisitic
$A$ be an indecomposable self-injective cellular algebra over $K$
conclusions: $A$ is Morita equivalent to one of the following symmetric algebras
the algebras (1) are of finite type,  the algebras (2)-(6) are of domestic infinite type, the algebras (7) are nondomestic of polynomial growth
any indecomposable self-injective cellular algebra of polynomial growth is of the form $fM_n(A)f$
nodes.statement_short: Over an algebraically closed field of odd characteristic, indecomposable self-injective cellular algebras of polynomial growth are Morita equivalent to one of seven explicit families.

nodes.name: Assembly of the main theorem
nodes.statement:
The algebras (1) are from Theorem \ref{F Theorem}, the algebra (2) is from Proposition \ref{D prop local} and Proposition \ref{D I-2 cellular}, 
the algebra (3) is from Proposition \ref{D I-2 cellular}, the algebras (4) are from Proposition \ref{D II} 
and Lemma \ref{D V-5}, the algebra (5) is from Lemma \ref{D V-5}, 
the algebras (6) are from Proposition \ref{D IV}, and the classification results from (2)-(6) are
summarized in Theorem \ref{D main result}. The classification (7) is Theorem \ref{P main}.
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Combine the finite, domestic and nondomestic classification results of Sections 3-5.

nodes.name: Module category A-mod
nodes.statement:
For a finite dimensional algebra $A$ over a field $K$, 
we denote  the category of finite dimensional left $A$-modules by $A \operatorname{-mod}$.
nodes.section: Introduction

nodes.name: Composition multiplicity

For an $A$-module $M$ and a simple $A$-module $L$, 
we denote the composition multiplicity of $L$ in $M$ by $[M:L]$.

nodes.name: Finite quiver
nodes.statement:
Let $Q =(Q_0,Q_1)$ be a finite quiver, 
where $Q_0$ is the set of vertices and $Q_1$ is the set of arrows.
nodes.section: Introduction

nodes.name: Bound quiver algebra KQ/I
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be an admissible ideal of the path algebra $K Q$ of $Q$ over a field $K$, so that $A:=K Q/I$ is a finite dimensional $K$-algebra.
nodes.section: Introduction

nodes.name: Idempotents, simples and projectives at vertices
nodes.statement:
For a vertex $i \in Q_0$, we denote by $e_i$ the corresponding primitive idempotent of $A$, 
and by $L_i$ (resp. $P_i$) the corresponding simple (resp. indecomposable projective) $A$-module.
nodes.section: Introduction

nodes.name: Cellular algebra
nodes.statement:
An associative algebra $A$ over a field $K$ is called a \emph{cellular algebra} with cell datum $(\varLambda, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \iota)$ 
if the following conditions are satisfied: 
\begin{description}
\item[(C1)] 
$\varLambda$ is a finite partially ordered set with a partial order $\geq$.  
For each $\lambda \in \varLambda$, there exists a finite set $\mathcal{T}(\lambda)$ such that
the algebra $A$ has a $K$-basis 
\begin{align*} 
\mathcal{C} =\{c_{\mathfrak s \mathfrak t}^{\lambda} \mid \mathfrak s, \mathfrak t \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda), \, \lambda \in \varLambda\}. 
\end{align*}

\item[(C2)] 
The linear map $\iota : A \rightarrow A$ which sends $c_{\mathfrak s \mathfrak t}^{\lambda}$ to $c_{\mathfrak t \mathfrak s}^{\lambda}$ ($\mathfrak s, \mathfrak t \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)$, $\lambda \in \varLambda$) 
gives an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$. 
(Clearly, $\iota$ is an involution.)

\item[(C3)] 
For any $\lambda \in \varLambda$, $\mathfrak s \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)$ and $a \in A$, there exist $r_{\mathfrak u}^{(a, \mathfrak s)} \in K$ ($\mathfrak u\in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)$) such that 
\begin{align} a c_{\mathfrak s \mathfrak t}^{\lambda} \equiv \sum_{\mathfrak u \in\mathcal{T}(\lambda)} r_{\mathfrak u}^{(a, \mathfrak s)} c_{\mathfrak u \mathfrak t}^{\lambda} \mod A^{>\lambda}, 
\end{align}
where $A^{> \lambda}$ is a subspace of $A$ spanned by 
$\{ c_{\mathfrak s' \mathfrak t'}^{\lambda'} \mid \mathfrak s', \mathfrak t' \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda'), \,  \lambda' > \lambda, \lambda' \in \varLambda\}$, 
and $r_{\mathfrak u}^{(a,\mathfrak s)}$ does not depend on $\mathfrak t$. 
\end{description}
The above basis $\mathcal{C}$ is called a \emph{cellular basis}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: An algebra with a basis indexed by a poset and pairs of tableaux, an anti-involution swapping indices, and a triangular multiplication rule modulo higher cells.

nodes.name: Cellular multiplication rule (C3)
nodes.statement: a c_{\mathfrak s \mathfrak t}^{\lambda} \equiv \sum_{\mathfrak u \in\mathcal{T}(\lambda)} r_{\mathfrak u}^{(a, \mathfrak s)} c_{\mathfrak u \mathfrak t}^{\lambda} \mod A^{>\lambda},
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.label: C a cst

nodes.name: Right multiplication rule
nodes.statement: c_{\mathfrak t \mathfrak s}^{\lambda} a \equiv \sum_{\mathfrak u \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)} r_{\mathfrak u}^{(\iota(a), \mathfrak s)} c_{\mathfrak t \mathfrak u}^{\lambda} \mod A^{>\lambda}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.label: C cts a

nodes.name: Cell module Delta(lambda) as a vector space with A-action
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a cellular algebra with cell datum $(\varLambda, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \iota)$. 
For each $\lambda \in \varLambda$,  
let $\Delta(\lambda)$ be a $K$-vector space with a basis $\{c_{\mathfrak s}^{\lambda} \mid \mathfrak s \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)\}$. 
We can define an action of $A$ on $\Delta(\lambda)$ by 
\begin{align*}
a \cdot c_{\mathfrak s}^{\lambda} = \sum_{\mathfrak u \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)} r_{\mathfrak u}^{(a, \mathfrak s)} c_{\mathfrak u}^{\lambda}, 
\end{align*}
where $r_{\mathfrak u}^{(a, \mathfrak s)} \in K$ are those coefficients given in \eqref{C a cst}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Cell modules
nodes.statement: We call the $A$-modules $\Delta(\lambda)$ ($\lambda \in \varLambda$) \emph{cell modules}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Product of cell basis elements
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
conclusions: $r_{\mathfrak s \mathfrak t}\in K $ does not depend on $\mathfrak u$ and $\mathfrak v$

nodes.name: Bilinear form on a cell module
nodes.statement: Then we define a bilinear form $\langle \, , \, \rangle$ on $\Delta(\lambda)$ by $\langle c_{\mathfrak s}^{\lambda}, c_{\mathfrak t}^{\lambda} \rangle = r_{\mathfrak s \mathfrak t}$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Radical of the bilinear form
nodes.statement: Let $\operatorname{rad}_{\langle \,,\,\rangle} \Delta(\lambda)$ be the radical of the bilinear form $\langle \,,\, \rangle$ on $\Delta(\lambda)$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Radical of the cell form is a submodule
nodes.statement: Then $\operatorname{rad}_{\langle \,,\, \rangle} \Delta(\lambda)$ is an $A$-submodule of $\Delta(\lambda)$ by \cite[Proposition 3.2]{GL}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Simple heads L(lambda) and Lambda^+
nodes.statement:
Put $L(\lambda) = \Delta(\lambda) / \operatorname{rad}_{\langle \,,\, \rangle} \Delta(\lambda)$, 
and $ \varLambda^+ = \{\lambda \in \varLambda \mid L(\lambda) \not=0\}$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Simple modules of a cellular algebra
nodes.statement:
\ \begin{enumerate}
\item 
For $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$, $L(\lambda)$ is absolutely irreducible. 

\item 
The set $\{L(\lambda) \mid \lambda \in \varLambda^+\}$ is a complete set of representatives of isomorphism classes of simple $A$-modules. 

\item 
For $\lambda, \mu \in \varLambda^+$, we have 
$\dim_K \operatorname{Ext}_{A}^i (L(\lambda), L(\mu)) = \dim_K \operatorname{Ext}_{A}^i (L(\mu), L(\lambda))$ for all $i \geq 0$. 

\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
conclusions: The set $\{L(\lambda) \mid \lambda \in \varLambda^+\}$ is a complete set of representatives of isomorphism classes of simple $A$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: The L(lambda) are absolutely irreducible, classify the simples, and Ext dimensions between simples are symmetric.
nodes.label: C Prop simple

nodes.name: Arrows of a cellular quiver have inverses
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
assumptions: a cellular algebra $A$ has the bounded quiver presentation $KQ_A/I$
conclusions: each arrow of $Q_A$ must have the inverse arrow

nodes.name: Justification of the Brauer graph branch criterion
nodes.statement:
We note that the five classes of algebras we will consider in \S3 are 
defined in the form $KQ/I$ but $I$ are not admissible in the first place, so that we must rewrite them when we apply Proposition \ref{C Prop simple}(iii).
However, in our application, we will see that the rewriting is merely deletion of the loops in the quiver $Q$ which come from vertices of valency 
one in Brauer graphs we start with.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Rewriting the non-admissible presentations only deletes loops from valency-one vertices.

nodes.name: Branch criterion for cellular Brauer-graph type algebras
nodes.statement:
Hence, Proposition \ref{C Prop simple}(iii) implies that if one of the algebras we consider in \S3 is cellular, then 
either there is no branch in the Brauer graph or 
there is one loop and the endpoint of the loop is the only branch in the Brauer graph whose valency at most four.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: If such an algebra is cellular, its Brauer graph has no branch, or one loop whose endpoint is the only branch point.

nodes.name: Decomposition numbers
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Decomposition matrix
nodes.statement: Put $\mathbf D=(d_{\lambda \mu})_{\lambda \in \varLambda, \mu \in \varLambda^+}$, and we call it the \emph{decomposition matrix}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Projective cover P(lambda)
nodes.statement: For $\lambda\in \varLambda^+$, let $P(\lambda)$ be the projective cover of $L(\lambda)$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Cartan matrix
nodes.statement:
Let $c_{\lambda\mu} = [P(\lambda) : L(\mu)]$, for $\lambda, \mu \in \varLambda^+$, and put $\mathbf C =(c_{\lambda \mu})_{\lambda,\mu \in \varLambda^+}$. 
Then $\mathbf C$ is the \emph{Cartan matrix} of $A$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Enumeration along a linear extension
nodes.statement:
First, 
we enumerate the elements of $\varLambda$ as $\{\mu_1,\mu_2,\dots \}$ following a chosen linear extension. Hence $i < j$ if $\mu_i < \mu_j$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Ideals A(mu_i)
nodes.statement:
Next,
let $A(\mu_i)$ be the subspace of $A$ spanned by $\{c_{\mathfrak s \mathfrak t}^{\mu_k} \mid \mathfrak s, \mathfrak t \in \mathcal{T}(\mu_k), \, k \geq i\}$, for $\mu_i \in \varLambda$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: A(mu_i) is a two-sided ideal
nodes.statement: Then $A(\mu_i)$, for $1\le i \le |\varLambda|$, where $|\varLambda|$ is the size of $\varLambda$, is a two-sided ideal of $A$ by \eqref{C a cst} and \eqref{C cts a}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Sequence of cell ideals
nodes.statement:
Defining $ A(\mu_{|\varLambda|+1})$ to be $0$, 
we have the following sequence of two-sided ideals associated with the linear extension
\begin{align} A= A(\mu_1) \supset A(\mu_2) \supset \dots \supset A(\mu_{|\varLambda|}) \supset A(\mu_{|\varLambda|+1})=0.
\end{align}
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.definiendum: sequence of two-sided ideals associated with the linear extension

nodes.name: Filtration of A by cell ideals
nodes.statement: A= A(\mu_1) \supset A(\mu_2) \supset \dots \supset A(\mu_{|\varLambda|}) \supset A(\mu_{|\varLambda|+1})=0.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.label: C seq A

nodes.name: Induced filtration of P(lambda)
nodes.statement:
For each $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$, applying the exact functor $- \otimes_{A} P(\lambda)$ to \eqref{C seq A}, 
we have a sequence of $A$-submodules 
\begin{align} P(\lambda) = P(\lambda)_{\mu_1} \supset P(\lambda)_{\mu_2} \supset \dots \supset P(\lambda)_{\mu_{|\varLambda|}} \supset P(\lambda)_{\mu_{|\varLambda|}+1}=0, 
\end{align}
where we put $P(\lambda)_{\mu_i} = A(\mu_i) \otimes_{A} P(\lambda)$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Filtration of P(lambda)
nodes.statement: P(\lambda) = P(\lambda)_{\mu_1} \supset P(\lambda)_{\mu_2} \supset \dots \supset P(\lambda)_{\mu_{|\varLambda|}} \supset P(\lambda)_{\mu_{|\varLambda|}+1}=0,
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.label: C seq Pla

nodes.name: Decomposition matrix properties of cellular algebras
nodes.statement:
\ \begin{enumerate} 
\item 
For $\lambda \in \varLambda$ and $\mu \in \varLambda^+$, 
if $d_{\lambda\mu} \not=0$, then we have $\lambda \geq \mu$. 
Moreover, if $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$, we have $d_{\lambda \lambda} =1$. 

\item 
For $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$ and the $A$-submodules $P(\lambda)_{\mu_i}$ in the sequence \eqref{C seq Pla}, we have 
$P(\lambda)_{\mu_i}/ P(\lambda)_{\mu_{i+1}} \cong \Delta(\mu_i)^{\oplus d_{\mu_i \lambda}}$ 
as $A$-modules. 

\item 
We have 
$\mathbf C= \mathbf D^T \mathbf D$, where $\mathbf D^T$ is the transpose of $\mathbf D$. 

\item 
We have $\det \mathbf C >0$. 

\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Decomposition matrix is unitriangular w.r.t. the order, cell filtrations of projectives, C = D^T D, and det C > 0.
nodes.label: C Prop decom matrix

nodes.name: Morita invariance and weak symmetry of cellular algebras
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a cellular algebra over a field $K$. 
Then we have the following. 
\begin{enumerate} 
\item
If $\operatorname{char} K \not=2$ then the basic algebra $B$ of $A$ is also cellular and 
there is a Morita equivalence between $A$ and $B$ which respects the cellular structure.

\item 
If $A$ is self-injective then $A$ is weakly symmetric. 

\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
assumptions: $A$ be a cellular algebra over a field $K$
conclusions: the basic algebra $B$ of $A$ is also cellular and  there is a Morita equivalence between $A$ and $B$ which respects the cellular structure
the basic algebra $B$ of $A$ is also cellular and  there is a Morita equivalence between $A$ and $B$ which respects the cellular structure

nodes.label: C Prop Morita equiv

nodes.name: Reduction to basic algebras
nodes.statement:
Thanks to Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ichi}), 
it is enough to consider basic algebras in order to determine Morita equivalence classes of cellular algebras  
if the characteristic of the base field is odd.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Endomorphism algebras of projectives over cellular algebras are cellular
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $A$ is a cellular algebra over a field $K$ of odd characteristic. If $P$ is a finitely generated projective $A$-module, 
then $\operatorname{End}_A(P)$ is a cellular algebra.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
assumptions: $A$ is a cellular algebra over a field $K$ of odd characteristic
nodes.label: C Lem idem

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the idempotent lemma (Remark)
nodes.statement:
For the proof, let $Q$ be the direct sum of pairwise inequivalent indecomposable projective $A$-modules that appear 
as direct summands of $P$. Then the opposite algebra of $\operatorname{End}_A(Q)$ is of the form $eAe$, for an idempotent $e\in A$. 
We may prove that $eAe$ is a cellular algebra. As $\operatorname{End}_A(Q)$ is the basic algebra of $\operatorname{End}_A(P)$, we have the isomorphism of algebras
$\operatorname{End}_A(P)\cong fM_n(\operatorname{End}_A(Q))f$, for an idempotent $f$ of the matrix algebra $M_n(\operatorname{End}_A(Q))$. 
Noting that a matrix algebra over a cellular algebra is a cellular algebra, we deduce that $\operatorname{End}_A(P)$ is a cellular algebra by the same argument 
which we used to prove that $eAe$ is a cellular algebra.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Reduce End_A(P) to the basic algebra eAe, then use that matrix algebras over cellular algebras are cellular.

nodes.name: Corner algebras of cellular algebras are cellular
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a cellular algebra over a field of odd characteristic, then $e A e$ is a cellular algebra for any idempotent $e \in A$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
assumptions: $A$ is a cellular algebra over a field of odd characteristic
conclusions: $e A e$ is a cellular algebra for any idempotent $e \in A$

nodes.name: Cellularity from a Morita equivalent corner
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite dimensional algebra over a field of odd characteristic, 
and suppose that $eAe$, for an idempotent $e \in A$, and $A$ are Morita equivalent. 
Then, $A$ is a cellular algebra if $eAe$ is a cellular algebra.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
assumptions: $A$ be a finite dimensional algebra over a field of odd characteristic
$eAe$, for an idempotent $e \in A$, and $A$ are Morita equivalent

nodes.name: Cellularity is Morita invariant in odd characteristic
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $\operatorname{char} K \not=2$ and let $A$ be a finite dimensional $K$-algebra. Then, $A$ is a cellular algebra if and only if 
its basic algebra is a cellular algebra.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
conclusions:
$A$ is a cellular algebra if and only if 
its basic algebra is a cellular algebra
equivalent_conditions: $A$ is a cellular algebra
its basic algebra is a cellular algebra

nodes.name: Proof of consequence (b)
nodes.statement:
For the second statement, we recall that the functor $F:=eA\otimes_A-$ induces 
the equivalence and $Ae\otimes_{eAe}eA\cong A$ holds. Thus, $eA=F(A)$ is a finitely generated projective $eAe$-module and 
$\operatorname{End}_{eAe}(eA)\cong \operatorname{End}_A(A)\cong A^{\rm op}$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: eA is a finitely generated projective eAe-module with endomorphism ring A^op; apply the lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of consequence (c)
nodes.statement: The third statement follows from Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ichi}) and (b).
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Combine Morita invariance of cellularity (KX2) with (b).

nodes.name: Minimal and maximal cells of self-injective cellular algebras
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a cellular algebra over a field $K$ with cell datum $(\varLambda, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \iota)$. 
Then we have the following. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
If $\lambda \in \varLambda$ is minimal, 
then $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$, $d_{\lambda \lambda }=1$ and $d_{\lambda \mu}=0$ for all $\mu \in \varLambda^+ \setminus \{\lambda\}$. 

\item 
Assume that $A$ is self-injective. 
If $\lambda \in \varLambda$ is maximal, 
then there exists $\mu \in \varLambda^+$ such that 
$d_{\lambda \mu}=1$ and $d_{\lambda \nu}=0$ for all $\nu \in \varLambda^+ \setminus \{ \mu\}$. 
In particular, if $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$ then $d_{\lambda \nu}=0$ for all $\nu \in \varLambda^+ \setminus \{ \lambda\}$.

\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
assumptions: $A$ be a cellular algebra over a field $K$ with cell datum $(\varLambda, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \iota)$
conclusions: there exists $\mu \in \varLambda^+$ such that  $d_{\lambda \mu}=1$ and $d_{\lambda \nu}=0$ for all $\nu \in \varLambda^+ \setminus \{ \mu\}$
there exists $\mu \in \varLambda^+$ such that  $d_{\lambda \mu}=1$ and $d_{\lambda \nu}=0$ for all $\nu \in \varLambda^+ \setminus \{ \mu\}$

nodes.statement_short: Rows of the decomposition matrix for minimal cells, and for maximal cells of self-injective cellular algebras, are unit vectors.
nodes.label: C Lem min

nodes.name: Proof of the minimal/maximal cell lemma
nodes.statement:
(\roman{ichi}) follows from Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ichi}) immediately. 
We prove (\roman{ni}). 
Since we assume that $A$ is a self-injective cellular algebra, 
$A$ is a weakly symmetric algebra by Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ni}). 

Let $\lambda \in \varLambda$ be maximal and choose a linear extension which ends with $\lambda$. 
Assume that there exists $\mu \in \varLambda^+$ such that $d_{\lambda \mu} \geq 2$. 
Then, by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ni}), 
we see that $P(\mu)$ contains $\Delta(\lambda)^{\oplus d_{\lambda \mu}}$ as an $A$-submodule, 
which implies that $\operatorname{Soc} P(\mu)$ is not irreducible. It contradicts with 
$\operatorname{Top} P(\mu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} P(\mu) \cong L(\mu)$. 
Thus, we have $d_{\lambda \mu} \leq 1$ for all $\mu \in \varLambda^+$. 
Next, assume that there exist $\mu, \nu \in \varLambda^+$ ($\mu \not=\nu$) 
such that $d_{\lambda \mu}= d_{\lambda \nu}=1$. 
Then, by the same reasoning, both $P(\mu)$ and $P(\nu)$ contain $\Delta(\lambda)$ as an $A$-submodule. It follows that 
we have 
$L(\mu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} P(\mu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} \Delta(\lambda)$ 
and 
$L(\nu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} P(\nu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} \Delta(\lambda)$. 
However, $L(\mu)$ and $L(\nu)$ are inequivalent $A$-modules by Proposition \ref{C Prop simple} (ii).
Thus, we have (\roman{ni}).

nodes.statement_short: Part (i) from unitriangularity; part (ii) by contradiction using simple socles of projectives of a weakly symmetric algebra.

$A$ is a weakly symmetric algebra by Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ni}).

nodes.name: Strategy 1: reduce to Skowronski's list
nodes.statement:
By Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ichi}) and our assumption that $\operatorname{char} K \not=2$, 
it is enough to classify basic self-injective cellular algebras of polynomial growth 
up to isomorphism of algebras.  
Since basic self-injective algebras over an algebraically closed field of polynomial growth 
have been classified by several authors, 
and they are listed in \cite{S}, 
it is enough to specify cellular algebras in the list of algebras from \cite{S}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Strategy 2: exhibit a cellular basis
nodes.statement:
In order to prove that a basic algebra listed in \cite{S} is cellular,
it is enough to give a cellular basis explicitly.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Strategy 3: contradiction on a small corner algebra
nodes.statement:
In order to prove that a basic algebra listed in \cite{S} is not cellular, 
it is enough to give a contradiction to a property of cellular algebras given in this section 
for a cellular algebra with a small number of simple modules which is obtained from the original basic algebra 
by applying Lemma \ref{C Lem idem}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Standing assumption: algebraically closed field of characteristic not 2
nodes.statement:
Throughout the paper, 
we always assume that $K$ is an algebraically closed field of $\operatorname{char} K \not=2$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
also_stated_at: To assure that cellularity is a Morita invariant property,  we assume that the base field has an odd characteristic throughout the paper.

nodes.name: Self-injective algebras of finite type are standard
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Theorem 3.8]{S} and $\operatorname{char} K \not=2$, the self-injective algebras we consider in this section are standard, 
that is, it admits a simply connected Galois covering whose Galois group is an admissible torsion-free group of $K$-linear automorphisms.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type

nodes.name: Classification of standard symmetric algebras of finite type
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Theorem 3.11]{S}, 
a nonsimple basic standard symmetric algebra of finite type is isomorphic to one of the following algebras: 
\begin{itemize}
\item 
A Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree has at most one exceptional vertex. 

\item 
A modified Brauer tree algebra $D(T_S)$ 
associated to a Brauer tree $T_S$ 
with at least two edges and an extreme exceptional vertex $S$ of multiplicity $2$. 

\item 
A trivial extension $T(B)$ of a tilted algebra $B$ of Dynkin type.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Nonsimple basic standard symmetric algebras of finite type are Brauer tree algebras, modified Brauer tree algebras, or trivial extensions of tilted Dynkin algebras.

nodes.name: Brauer tree algebra and modified Brauer tree algebra notation
nodes.statement:
For the definitions of a Brauer tree algebra, which we denote by $A(T^m_S)$ if it has an exceptional vertex $S$ 
of multiplicity $m\ge2$, and a modified Brauer tree algebra $D(T_S)$, 
see \cite[paragraphs 2.8 and 3.6]{S}.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type

nodes.name: Cellularity of Brauer tree algebras
nodes.statement:
A Brauer tree algebra is cellular 
if and only if
the Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
also_stated_at: a result from K\"onig and Xi \cite{KX1}, which states that a Brauer tree algebra is cellular  if and only if the Brauer tree is a straight line (with at most one exceptional vertex)
conclusions: A Brauer tree algebra is cellular  if and only if the Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex
equivalent_conditions: A Brauer tree algebra is cellular
the Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex
nodes.label: F Prop BT

nodes.name: Remark on exceptional vertices in KX1
nodes.statement:
In \cite[Proposition 5.3]{KX1}, 
Brauer trees are allowed to have an arbitrary number of exceptional vertices. 
However, in the above classification of nonsimple basic standard symmetric algebras of finite type, 
we consider only  Brauer trees with at most one exceptional vertex $S$.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type

nodes.name: Argument that T_S is a straight line
nodes.statement:
We consider a modified Brauer tree algebra $D(T_S)$. 
By the definition of $D(T_S)$, 
if the Brauer tree $T_S$ has a branch, 
then the quiver of $D(T_S)$ contains a cycle whose length is at least $3$, 
and this cycle has no inverse arrow. 
This contradicts Proposition \ref{C Prop simple} (\roman{san}) if $D(T_S)$ is cellular.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: A branch yields a cycle of length >= 3 without inverse arrows, contradicting Ext-symmetry.

nodes.name: Cellular modified Brauer tree algebras have straight-line trees
nodes.statement:
Thus, we see that 
the Brauer tree $T_S$ is a straight line if $D(T_S)$ is cellular.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
conclusions: the Brauer tree $T_S$ is a straight line

nodes.name: The 10-dimensional two-vertex algebra is not cellular
nodes.statement:
Let $A=KQ / I$ where
\[
\xymatrix{Q = & 1 \ar@(ul,dl)_{\gamma } \ar[r]<0.5 ex>^{\alpha_1}  & 2 \ar[l]<0.5 ex>^{\beta_1}}
\]
and $I$ is the two-sided ideal generated by 
$\{ \beta_1 \alpha_1, \, \gamma^2 - \alpha_1 \beta_1\}$. 
Then, $\dim A = 10$ and $A$ is not cellular.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
assumptions: $I$ is the two-sided ideal generated by  $\{ \beta_1 \alpha_1, \, \gamma^2 - \alpha_1 \beta_1\}$
nodes.label: F Lemma DB 2

nodes.name: Proof that the algebra KQ/(beta_1 alpha_1, gamma^2-alpha_1 beta_1) is not cellular
nodes.statement:
We see that 
\begin{align*}
& A e_1 = K e_1 \oplus K \gamma \oplus K \beta_1 \oplus K \gamma^2 \oplus K \beta_1 \gamma \oplus K \gamma^3, 
\\
& A e_2 = K e_2 \oplus K \alpha_1 \oplus K \gamma \alpha_1 \oplus K \beta_1 \gamma \alpha_1, 
\end{align*} 
and the Cartan matrix of $A$ is
\[
\mathbf C= \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. 
\]
Suppose that $A$ is a cellular algebra with cell datum $(\varLambda, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \iota)$. 
Let $\mathbf D$ be the decomposition matrix of the cellular structure of $A$. 
Then, by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{san}), 
we have 
\[
\mathbf D^T \mathbf D = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. 
\]
As Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ichi}) tells us that every column of $D$ must contain $1$ as an entry, this equation implies that 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf D= (d_{ij})_{1\leq i \leq 4, 1 \leq j \leq 2}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1& 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\end{align*} 
modulo rearrangement of rows.  
Let $\varLambda=\{\lambda_1,\lambda_2, \lambda_3,\lambda_4\}$ and $\varLambda^+=\{ \mu_1, \mu_2\}$ be  such that 
$[ \Delta(\lambda_i) : L(\mu_j) ] = d_{ij}$. If $\lambda_1$ or $\lambda_2$ was maximal or minimal with respect to the partial order, then 
the corresponding row of $D$ would be a unit vector by Lemma \ref{C Lem min}, a contradiction. Thus, 
we can assume that 
a total order on $\varLambda$ which extends the partial order is 
$3<1<2<4$. In particular, we do not have $\lambda_1>\lambda_2$ in the partial order. 
We also note that $\mu = \min\{ \lambda \in \varLambda \mid d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0 \}$, for $\mu\in \varLambda^+$, by 
Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ichi}). As $d_{\lambda_i\mu_2}\ne0$ only for $i=1,2$, $\mu_2\in\{\lambda_1,\lambda_2\}$, but
$\mu_2=\lambda_2$ contradicts $\lambda_1\not>\lambda_2$, so that $\mu_2=\lambda_1$. The minimality of $\lambda_3$ implies
$\mu_1=\lambda_3$ by Lemma \ref{C Lem min}(i).

We determine $A(\lambda_4)$ and $A(\lambda_2)$. By Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ni}), 
we see that 
\begin{align} A(\lambda_4) e_1 \cong P(\mu_1)_{\lambda_4} \cong \Delta(\lambda_4), 
\quad 
A(\lambda_4) e_2 \cong P(\mu_2)_{\lambda_4} =0. 
\end{align}
As $A (\lambda_4)$ is a two-sided-ideal and $\Delta(\lambda_4) \cong L(\mu_1)$, 
\eqref{F DB 2} implies that $A(\lambda_4) = K \gamma^3$. 
In a similar way, we see that 
\begin{align} \begin{split}
&(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4) )e_1 \cong P(\mu_1)_{\lambda_2} / P(\mu_1)_{\lambda_4} \cong \Delta(\lambda_2), 
\\
&(A(\lambda_2) / A(\lambda_4)) e_2 \cong P(\mu_2)_{\lambda_2} / P(\mu_2)_{\lambda_4} \cong \Delta(\lambda_2). 
\end{split}
\end{align}
Note that $A (\lambda_2)$ is a two-sided-ideal and $[ \Delta(\lambda_2) ] = [L(\mu_1)] + [L(\mu_2)]$.  
Then, since $\dim e_1(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4) )e_1 = 1$, there is a nonzero element $ae_1+b\gamma+c\gamma^2$ in $A(\lambda_2)e_1$. If $a\ne0$ 
then $a\gamma+b\gamma^2 \in A(\lambda_2)e_1$, which implies $\dim e_1(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4) )e_1>1$. 
Thus, $a=0$. The same argument shows $b=0$ and we conclude that $\gamma^2\in A(\lambda_2)e_1$. On the other hand, $\dim e_2(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4) )e_1 = 1$
implies that there is a nonzero element $a\beta_1+b\beta_1\gamma$ in $A(\lambda_2)e_1$. 
We may also prove $\beta_1\gamma\alpha_1 \in A(\lambda_2)e_2$ and $\gamma\alpha_1 \in A(\lambda_2)e_2$ in the similar manner. Hence,
\begin{align*}
&(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4)) e_1 \equiv K \gamma^2 \oplus K (a\beta_1 + b\beta_1\gamma) \mod A (\lambda_4), 
\\ 
&(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4))e_2 \equiv K \gamma \alpha_1 \oplus K \beta_1 \gamma \alpha_1 \mod A (\lambda_4).
\end{align*}
We observe that $\alpha_1$ acts as zero on $(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4))e_2$. Then, $\alpha_1(a\beta_1 + b\beta_1\gamma) \equiv a\gamma^2$ implies $a=0$. 
However, if $a=0$ then we meet another contradiction
\begin{align*}
&\operatorname{Soc} \Delta(\lambda_2) \cong \operatorname{Soc} (A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4)) e_1 \cong L(\mu_1) \oplus L(\mu_2), 
\\ 
&\operatorname{Soc} \Delta(\lambda_2) \cong  \operatorname{Soc} (A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4))e_2 \cong  L(\mu_2).
\end{align*}
We have proved that $A$ is not cellular.

nodes.name: Modified Brauer tree algebras are not cellular
nodes.statement:
A modified Brauer tree algebra $D(T_S)$ 
associated to any Brauer tree $T_S$ 
with at least two edges and an extreme exceptional vertex $S$ of multiplicity $2$ 
is not cellular.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
assumptions: associated to any Brauer tree $T_S$  with at least two edges and an extreme exceptional vertex $S$ of multiplicity $2$
nodes.label: F Prop MBD

nodes.name: Proof that modified Brauer tree algebras are not cellular
nodes.statement:
If $D (T_S)$ is a cellular algebra, 
the Brauer tree $T_S$ has to be a straight line by the argument in \ref{F BD}. 
On the other hand, 
if $T_S$ is a straight line with $n$ edges, 
then we have $D(T_S) = KQ_{T_S}/ I_{T_S}$, 
where $Q_{T_S}$ and $I_{T_S}$ are given by \eqref{F QTS} and \eqref{F ITS} respectively. 
Moreover, if we denote the algebra from Lemma \ref{F Lemma DB 2} by $A$,
we see that $(e_1+e_2)D(T_S)(e_1+e_2) \cong A$. 
Indeed, if we compute bases of $D(T_S)e_1$ and $D(T_S)e_2$ explicitly, we know that 
$\dim (e_1+e_2)D(T_S)(e_1+e_2) = 10$ 
and that we have a surjective algebra homomorphism $A \to (e_1+e_2)D(T_S)(e_1+e_2)$. 
Thus, $(e_1+e_2)D(T_S)(e_1+e_2)$ is not cellular by Lemma \ref{F Lemma DB 2}, 
so that $D(T_S)$ is not cellular by Lemma \ref{C Lem idem}.

nodes.statement:

the Brauer tree $T_S$ has to be a straight line by the argument in \ref{F BD}.

then we have $D(T_S) = KQ_{T_S}/ I_{T_S}$, 
where $Q_{T_S}$ and $I_{T_S}$ are given by \eqref{F QTS} and \eqref{F ITS} respectively.

Thus, $(e_1+e_2)D(T_S)(e_1+e_2)$ is not cellular by Lemma \ref{F Lemma DB 2},

nodes.name: Tilted algebras of Dynkin type have acyclic quivers
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Corollary 3.4 in Chapter VIII]{ASS}, 
The quiver of $B$ is acyclic.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type

nodes.name: Cellular trivial extensions of acyclic algebras are radical-square-zero
nodes.statement:
Let $Q$ be a finite acyclic quiver, 
$I$ an admissible ideal of $K Q$. 
Put $A= KQ/I$. 
If the trivial extension $T(A)$ of $A$ is cellular, 
then we have $I= R^2_Q$, 
where $R_Q$ is the arrow ideal of $KQ$.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
assumptions: the trivial extension $T(A)$ of $A$ is cellular
nodes.label: F Lemma TA

nodes.name: Proof of the trivial extension lemma
nodes.statement:
We consider a bounded quiver presentation of $T(A)$. 
For this, we need add new arrows to $Q$ which generate $\operatorname{Hom}_K(A,K)$. 
Then, we obtain 
the quiver $Q_{T(A)}$ of $T(A)$ from the quiver of $Q$ by the following 
recipe\footnote{Since $T(A)$ is the quotient of the repetitive algebra 
by the Nakayama automorphism $\nu_A$, 
we may also obtain the presentation by 
using the bounded quiver presentation of the repetitive algebra of $A$ 
given in \cite[Lemma 1.3]{A}.}: 
\begin{quote}
\it
Let $\alpha$ be a path in $Q$ such that $\alpha \not \in I$ and $\beta \alpha, \alpha \beta \in I$ for any arrow $\beta$ in $Q$.
Then we add an arrow from $t(\alpha)$ to $s(\alpha)$, 
where $t(\alpha)$ is the target of $\alpha$ and $s(\alpha)$ is the source of $\alpha$.  
\end{quote}
Thanks to this construction, 
if there exists a path $\alpha$ in $Q$ such that the length of $\alpha$ is at least $2$ and $\alpha \not\in I$, 
then $Q_{T(A)}$ contains a cycle whose length is at least $3$, 
and this cycle has no inverse arrow. 
This contradicts Proposition \ref{C Prop simple} (\roman{san}) if $T(A)$ is cellular. 
We have proved $R_Q^2\subset I$. 
The opposite inclusion is clear since $I$ is an admissible ideal.

nodes.statement_short: A path of length >= 2 not in I produces a cycle of length >= 3 in the quiver of T(A) without inverse arrows, contradicting Ext-symmetry.

nodes.name: Double quiver
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Lemma 1.3]{A} (see the proof of Lemma \ref{F Lemma TA}), 
we see that the quiver of $T(KQ/R_Q^2)$ is the double quiver 
$\widehat{Q}=(\widehat{Q}_0, \widehat{Q}_1)$ of $Q$, 
namely $\widehat{Q}_0=Q_0$ and $\widehat{Q}_1$ is obtained from $Q_1$ by adding an additional arrow $\alpha^*$ 
for each $\alpha \in Q_1$ such that $s(\alpha^*) = t(\alpha)$ and $t(\alpha^*)=s (\alpha)$.

nodes.name: Trivial extension of KQ/R_Q^2 as a bound double quiver algebra
nodes.statement:
Let $Q=(Q_0,Q_1)$ be a finite acyclic quiver, 
and $R_Q$ be the arrow ideal of $KQ$. 
Then the trivial extension $T(KQ/ R_Q^2)$ of $KQ/ R_Q^2$ 
is isomorphic to $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
conclusions: the trivial extension $T(KQ/ R_Q^2)$ of $KQ/ R_Q^2$  is isomorphic to $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$
nodes.label: F Lemma KQ RQ2

nodes.name: Proof of the trivial extension presentation
nodes.statement:
Let $\{f_{i} \mid i \in Q_0\} \cup \{ f_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in Q_1\} \subset \operatorname{Hom}_{K} (KQ/ R_Q^2, K)$ 
be the dual basis of the basis
$\{e_i \mid i \in Q_0\} \cup \{\alpha \in Q_1\}$ of $KQ/ R_Q^2$,
namely $f_{i}(e_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $f_{i}(\alpha)=0$, $f_{\alpha}(e_i)=0$ and $f_{\alpha}(\beta) = \delta_{\alpha \beta}$, 
for $i,j \in Q_0$ and $\alpha, \beta \in Q_1$. 
Then
\begin{align*}
\{e_i \mid i \in Q_0\} \cup \{\alpha \in Q_1\} \cup \{f_{i} \mid i \in Q_0\} \cup \{ f_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in Q_1\}
\end{align*}
gives a basis of $T(KQ/ R_Q^2)$. 
Checking the well-definedness by direct calculation,
we can define an algebra homomorphism $\Phi: K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}} \rightarrow T (KQ/ R_Q^2)$ by
\begin{align*} 
e_i \mapsto e_i \, (i \in Q_0), \, 
\alpha \mapsto \alpha, \, \alpha^* \mapsto f_{\alpha} \, (\alpha \in Q_1). 
\end{align*} 
In particular, we used
$\alpha f_{\alpha} = f_{s(\alpha)}$ and $f_\alpha \alpha = f_{t (\alpha)}$ in $T(KQ/ R_Q^2)$, for $\alpha \in Q_1$, 
in the calculation, and they also show that
$\Phi$ is surjective. 
By comparing the dimensions of $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ and $T(KQ/ R_Q^2)$, 
we see that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Cellularity of K hat Q / I_{hat Q}
nodes.statement:
Let $Q=(Q_0,Q_1)$ be a finite connected acyclic quiver. 
Then, 
the algebra 
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is cellular 
if and only if 
the underlying graph $\overline{Q}$ of $Q$ is a straight line with no multiple edge.
Furthermore, if the condition holds then
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is isomorphic to the Brauer tree algebra whose
Brauer tree is a straight line with no exceptional vertex.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
assumptions: $Q=(Q_0,Q_1)$ be a finite connected acyclic quiver
conclusions: the algebra  $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is cellular  if and only if  the underlying graph $\overline{Q}$ of $Q$ is a straight line with no multiple edge
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is isomorphic to the Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree is a straight line with no exceptional vertex
equivalent_conditions: the algebra  $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is cellular
the underlying graph $\overline{Q}$ of $Q$ is a straight line with no multiple edge
nodes.label: F Prop hatQ hatI

nodes.name: Proof of the cellularity criterion for K hat Q / I
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is cellular.
If $\overline{Q}$ has a multiple edge, 
then $Q$ contains a subquiver 
\[
\xymatrix{Q' =  i \ar[rr]<-1.5ex>   \ar[rr]<1.8ex> & \vdots  & j }
\]
with $k$ arrows ($k \geq 2$) by Proposition \ref{C Prop simple}.  
By the defining relations, 
we see that $(e_i + e_j)(K\widehat{Q} / I_{\widehat{Q}})(e_i + e_j) \cong K \widehat{Q'} / I_{\widehat{Q'}}$, 
and its Cartan matrix is
\[
\mathbf C'=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & k \\ k & 2 \end{pmatrix}. 
\]
By Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{yon}), 
$(e_i + e_j)(K\widehat{Q} / I_{\widehat{Q}})(e_i + e_j)$ is not cellular 
since $\det \mathbf C' \leq 0$. 
Then, by Lemma \ref{C Lem idem}, 
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is not cellular, contradicting our assumption. Hence
$\overline{Q}$ has no multiple edge. 

Note that $Q$ does not have an oriented cycle since $Q$ is acyclic. In particular 
the underlying graph of $Q$ does not contain a loop.
Suppose that $Q$ contains a subquiver $Q^{\sharp}$ 
whose underlying graph is a cycle of length $l\ge2$. We label its vertices as follows. 
\begin{align*}
\xymatrix@R=3pt{
&i_2 \ar@{-}[r] & i_3 \ar@{-}[dr]  &
\\
&&& \ar@{.}[dd]
\\
\overline{Q^{\sharp}} = i_1\ar@{-}[uur] &&& & 
\\
&&& \ar@{-}[dl]
\\
& i_l \ar@{-}[uul]& i_{l-1} \ar@{-}[l] &
}
\end{align*}
Then we see that 
$(e_{i_1} + \dots + e_{i_l}) (K\widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}) (e_{i_1} + \dots + e_{i_l}) 
	\cong K \widehat{Q^{\sharp}}/ I_{\widehat{Q^{\sharp}}}$, 
and its Cartan matrix is 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf C^{\sharp} = 
	\begin{pmatrix} 
	2 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 
	\\ 
	1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 
	\\
	0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 
	\\
	&&&&& \vdots &&&&
	\\
	0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1
	\\
	1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2
	\end{pmatrix}. 
\end{align*}
Suppose that $K \widehat{Q^{\sharp}}/ I_{\widehat{Q^{\sharp}}}$ is a cellular algebra with cell datum $(\varLambda,\mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \iota)$,  
and let $\mathbf D^{\sharp}$ be its decomposition matrix. 
Then, by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{san}), 
we have 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf D^{\sharp} = 
	\begin{pmatrix} 
	1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 1 
	\\
	1 & 1 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 
	\\
	0 & 1 & 1 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 
	\\
	&&&& \vdots &&&
        \\
        0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 1 & 1 & 0
	\\
	0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 1 & 1 
	\end{pmatrix}. 
\end{align*}
modulo rearrangement of rows.

Put $\varLambda =\{ \lambda_1, \lambda_2,\dots, \lambda_{l}\}$
such that $([\Delta(\lambda_i) : L(\lambda_j)])_{1\leq i,j \leq l} = \mathbf D^{\sharp}$.  
Then, by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ichi}), 
we have 
$\lambda_l < \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 < \dots < \lambda_{l-1} < \lambda_l$ in the partial order, which is impossible. Hence, 
$(e_{i_1} + \dots + e_{i_l}) (K\widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}) (e_{i_1} + \dots + e_{i_l})$ 
is not cellular, and 
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is not cellular by Lemma \ref{C Lem idem}, contradicting our assumption again.   

Assume that $\overline{Q}$ has no multiple edge and no cycle. 
If $\overline{Q}$ has a branch, 
$Q$ contains a subquiver $Q^{\natural}$ whose underlying graph is of the following form
\begin{align*}
&\xymatrix@R=5pt{ & & i_3 \\ \overline{Q^{\natural}} = i_1 \ar@{-}[r] & i_2 \ar@{-}[ur] \ar@{-}[dr] & & \\ && i_4}
\end{align*}
We see that 
$(e_{i_1}+ \dots + e_{i_4}) K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}} (e_{i_1}+ \dots + e_{i_4}) 
	\cong K \widehat{Q^{\natural}}/ I_{\widehat{Q^{\natural}}}$, 
and its Cartan matrix is 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf C^{\natural} = 
	\begin{pmatrix} 
	2 & 1 & 0 & 0 
	\\
	1 & 2 & 1 & 1 
	\\
	0 & 1 & 2 & 0 
	\\
	0 & 1 & 0 & 2
	\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align*} 
However, 
there is no matrix $\mathbf D$ with non-negative integral entries that satisfies 
$\mathbf D^T \mathbf D = \mathbf C$. 
Thus, 
$(e_{i_1}+ \dots + e_{i_4}) K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}} (e_{i_1}+ \dots + e_{i_4})$ 
is not cellular by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{san}), and 
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is not cellular by Lemma \ref{C Lem idem}. 

Now the only graph $\overline{Q}$ without cycles or loops, 
and branch points, is a straight line. Hence we have proved that 
$\overline{Q}$ is a straight line with no multiple edge if $K \widehat{Q} / I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is cellular. 

Conversely, suppose that $\overline{Q}$ is a straight line with no multiple edge. Then we easily see that 
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is isomorphic to the Brauer tree algebra 
whose Brauer tree is a straight line  
with no exceptional vertex, which is cellular by Proposition \ref{F Prop BT}.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Exclude multiple edges (det C <= 0), cycles (impossible cell order) and branches (no D with D^T D = C) on corner algebras; a straight line gives a Brauer tree algebra.

nodes.statement:

and branch points, is a straight line. Hence we have proved that

nodes.statement_short: A straight line gives a Brauer tree algebra, cellular by KX1.

nodes.name: Straight-line Brauer tree algebras are trivial extensions of type A

the Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree is a straight line with no exceptional vertex is
isomorphic to the trivial extension of a tilted algebra of type $A_n$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$.

nodes.statement:
The trivial extension $T(B)$ of a tilted algebra $B$ of Dynkin type 
is cellular 
if and only if 
$T(B)$ is isomorphic to the Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree is 
a straight line with no exceptional vertex.

nodes.statement:
By \cite[Theorem 3.11]{S}, Proposition \ref{F Prop BT}, Proposition \ref{F Prop MBD} and Proposition \ref{F Prop TE},

nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Run through Skowronski's list: Brauer tree algebras (KX1), modified Brauer tree algebras and trivial extensions.

nodes.name: Classification of basic symmetric cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement:
An algebra $A$ is a basic symmetric cellular algebra of finite type 
if and only if 
$A$ is isomorphic  to a Brauer tree algebra
whose Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
conclusions: $A$ is a basic symmetric cellular algebra of finite type  if and only if  $A$ is isomorphic  to a Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex

$A$ is isomorphic  to a Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex

nodes.name: Weakly symmetric algebras of finite type are symmetric
nodes.statement: A weakly symmetric algebra over $K$ of finite type is symmetric.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
assumptions: A weakly symmetric algebra over $K$ of finite type
nodes.label: F Prop weak

nodes.name: Proof via Stamm-algebras
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a basic weakly symmetric algebra over $K$ of finite type, 
and $A'$ be its Stamm-algebra (see \cite[Definition 4.4]{W} for the definition of Stamm-algebra). 
By \cite[Coroollary 4.7 (\roman{san}) in Part I]{W}, $A'$ is symmetric if and only if $A$ is weakly symmetric. 
If $A$ was not a symmetric algebra, then 
$A$ would be isomorphic to $A'$ by \cite[Theorem C]{KS}, 
which contradicts with $A'$ being a symmetric algebra.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Compare with the Stamm-algebra A', symmetric iff A is weakly symmetric; Kupisch-Scherzler forces A = A' otherwise.

nodes.name: Stamm-algebra
nodes.statement:

and $A'$ be its Stamm-algebra (see \cite[Definition 4.4]{W} for the definition of Stamm-algebra).

nodes.statement_short: Introduce the Stamm-algebra A' of A.

nodes.name: Waschbusch criterion
nodes.statement: By \cite[Coroollary 4.7 (\roman{san}) in Part I]{W}, $A'$ is symmetric if and only if $A$ is weakly symmetric.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: A' is symmetric iff A is weakly symmetric.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement:

$A$ would be isomorphic to $A'$ by \cite[Theorem C]{KS}, 
which contradicts with $A'$ being a symmetric algebra.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise A is isomorphic to A' by Kupisch-Scherzler, contradiction.

nodes.name: Proof of the finite type classification
nodes.statement:
By Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ni}), 
Proposition \ref{F Prop symmetric}
and 
Proposition \ref{F Prop weak}, 
we have the following theorem.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Self-injective cellular implies weakly symmetric, hence symmetric in finite type; then apply the symmetric classification.

nodes.name: Classification of self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a basic algebra over $K$. 
The following are equivalent. 
\begin{enumerate} 
\item 
$A$ is a self-injective cellular algebra of finite type. 

\item 
$A$ is isomorphic  to a Brauer tree algebra 
whose Brauer tree is
a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex. 
\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
equivalent_conditions: $A$ is a self-injective cellular algebra of finite type.
$A$ is isomorphic  to a Brauer tree algebra  whose Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex.
nodes.label: F Theorem

nodes.name: Reduction to weakly symmetric algebras with nonsingular Cartan matrix
nodes.statement:
By Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} and Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv},  
it suffices to consider weakly symmetric algebras of domestic type whose Cartan matrices are nonsingular.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of domestic type

nodes.name: Standard domestic self-injective algebras are of Euclidean type
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Theorem 4.3]{S}, a self-injective algebra is standard domestic of infinite type 
if and only if it is a self-injective algebra of Euclidean type.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of domestic type
equivalent_conditions: a self-injective algebra is standard domestic of infinite type
it is a self-injective algebra of Euclidean type
conclusions: a self-injective algebra is standard domestic of infinite type  if and only if it is a self-injective algebra of Euclidean type
